supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix a horizon $T>0$ and let
$\mathcal P_T$ be the predictable sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$
[[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Let $H$ be a
predictable process with
$$E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds=\int_{[0,T]\times\Omega}H^2\,d(\mathrm dt\otimes P)<\infty ,$$
so that $H$ is an element of the quotient space
$L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$ over $\mathcal P_T$; its class is what is integrated.
The **Ito integral** $\int_0^TH_s\,dB_s$, also written $H\cdot B$ or $I_T(H)$,
is defined as follows.

1. **Construction.** By the density theorem
   [[thm-density-of-elementary-predictable-processes-in-predictable-l2]] there
   is a sequence $(H^n)$ of bounded elementary predictable integrands
   [[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]] with
   $\|H^n-H\|_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)}\to0$. For such a sequence the
   elementary integrals $I_T(H^n)$
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]] form a Cauchy
   sequence in $L^2(P)$: by the elementary isometry
   [[thm-ito-isometry-for-elementary-integrands]] and the well-definedness of
   the elementary integral,
   $$E\bigl(I_T(H^n)-I_T(H^m)\bigr)^2=E\int_0^T(H^n-H^m)^2ds=\|H^n-H^m\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)} ,$$
   and the right-hand side tends to $0$. Since $L^2(P)$ is complete
   [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]], the classes $I_T(H^n)$ converge
   in $L^2(P)$; the limit is a class in $L^2(P)$, and
   $$\int_0^TH_s\,dB_s:=\lim_{n\to\infty}I_T(H^n)\qquad\text{in }L^2(P).$$
   The limit is a random variable only up to almost-sure equality; statements
   about it are statements about that class. The limit does not depend on the
   chosen sequence: if another elementary sequence $K^n\to H$ is used, then
   the elementary isometry and linearity give
   $$\|I_T(H^n)-I_T(K^n)\|_{L^2(P)} =\|H^n-K^n\|_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)} \le\|H^n-H\|_2+\|K^n-H\|_2\longrightarrow0,$$
   so the two $L^2(P)$ limits agree.

2. **Integrals at a time.** For $t\in[0,T]$ put
   $\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s:=\int_0^TH_s1_{[0,t]}(s)\,dB_s$, the construction of
   clause 1 applied to the truncated process $H1_{[0,t]}$. That process is
   predictable: $H$ is $\mathcal P_T$-measurable and $1_{[0,t]}$ is a
   deterministic predictable indicator, so the product is
   $\mathcal P_T$-measurable; and it is square-integrable because
   $|H1_{[0,t]}|\le|H|$ pointwise. The same construction applied to $H$
   itself gives $t=T$. The family
   $\bigl(\int_0^tH\,dB\bigr)_{t\in[0,T]}$ is a family of $L^2(P)$-classes
   indexed by $t$; its continuous version is supplied by item 13, and no path
   property is asserted by this definition.

3. **Consistency with elementary integrands.** If $H$ is itself elementary,
   then the constant sequence $H^n:=H$ is admissible in clause 1, so
   $\int_0^TH\,dB$ is the limit of the constant sequence of elementary sums,
   namely the elementary sum $I_T(H)$ of
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]]. The same argument
   with $H1_{[0,t]}$ in place of $H$, and the finite telescoping of the
   elementary sum over a refinement containing $t$, gives
   $\int_0^tH\,dB=I_t(H)$ for every $t\in[0,T]$. In particular the general
   definition extends, rather than replaces, the elementary definition.

4. **Linearity in the integrand is not asserted here.** Clause 1 defines each
   integral separately from an arbitrary approximating sequence; the linear and
   isometric properties of the extension are item 12. Until item 12 is proved,
   linearity may be used only for elementary integrands, where it is part of
   [[def-ito-integral-of-an-elementary-predictable-process]].

5. **Comparison with deterministic Riemann integration.** The integral is a
   stochastic integral: the integrand is paired with the Brownian path through
   left-endpoint sums and an $L^2(P)$ limit. This definition does not assert
   convergence of arbitrary tagged Riemann--Stieltjes sums for a general
   predictable integrand. Particular integrands can have a pathwise
   interpretation: for $H\equiv1$ every tagged sum telescopes to $B_T-B_0$,
   which is also its Ito integral by clause 3 (the value at time zero is
   irrelevant to its product-measure class). The notation $\int_0^TH\,dB$
   here always refers to the $L^2(P)$-class defined above.

The Axiom of Choice is declared because the construction selects an
approximating sequence and uses the completeness and conditional-expectation
interfaces that assume it; the inherited obligations are declared as
dependencies of this item. An alternative construction that avoids selecting the sequence is
not needed, because clause 1 shows every sequence gives the same class.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$. For predictable
$H,K$ with finite energy $E\int_0^TH^2ds,E\int_0^TK^2ds<\infty$ the integrals
$\int_0^TH\,dB$ of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] satisfy
$$\int_0^T(H+K)\,dB=\int_0^TH\,dB+\int_0^TK\,dB,\qquad \int_0^T(aH)\,dB=a\int_0^TH\,dB\quad(a\in\mathbb R),$$
and the identities are equalities of $L^2(P)$-classes (almost sure
equalities). Moreover the map $H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is an isometry,
$$E\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)^2=E\int_0^TH^2ds=\|H\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)},$$
it takes values in the mean-zero subspace of $L^2(P)$, and the bilinear cross
identity
$$E\Bigl[\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_0^TK\,dB\Bigr)\Bigr]=E\int_0^TH_sK_s\,ds$$
holds for all such $H,K$. In particular the image of the map is a closed
subspace of $L^2(P)$ isometric to the predictable $L^2$ space of $H$'s, and
$H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is injective up to the $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-class.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a predictable
process with $E\int_0^TH_s^2ds<\infty$ for every finite $T$. Then there is an
adapted process $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ with continuous paths such that
$M_t=\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ almost surely for every $t\ge0$
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]], and $M$ is a
square-integrable martingale relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]: $EM_t^2=E\int_0^tH_s^2ds<\infty$
for every $t$. Any two such continuous versions agree at every time on one
measurable event of probability one; in particular the continuous version is
unique in this common-full-measure-event sense, and it is the only continuous
square-integrable martingale whose value at each deterministic $t$ is the
integral class.

This conclusion is deliberately distinguished from the exact definition of
indistinguishability in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. On a
noncomplete probability space the full equality set, although it contains the
measurable probability-one event constructed below, need not itself be
measurable. On a complete probability space the two notions coincide, because
the complement of the equality set is then a measurable subset of a null set.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$ and let
$h\in L^2[0,T]$ be deterministic, choose a Borel representative of its
Lebesgue-equivalence class, and set $h(s,\omega):=h(s)$. This process is
predictable with finite energy. Then the Ito integral
$\int_0^Th_s\,dB_s$
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] is centered
normal with variance $\int_0^Th^2ds$: its law is $N(0,\int_0^Th^2ds)$ in the
convention of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]], where $N(0,0)$ is the
Dirac law at $0$. More generally, for deterministic $h_1,\dots,h_d\in L^2[0,T]$
the vector of integrals is jointly Gaussian in the sense of
[[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: its law is $N_d(0,\Sigma)$ with
$$\Sigma_{jk}=\int_0^Th_j(s)h_k(s)\,ds .$$
In particular the covariance of the pair is
$\operatorname{Cov}(\int h_jdB,\int h_kdB)=\int h_jh_k$, the integrals are
uncorrelated exactly when $\int h_jh_k=0$, and integrals of deterministic
integrands with disjoint supports are independent.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Fix $d\ge2$. The **elastic collision set** is
$$Q_{\rm el}:=\{(v,w,v',w')\in\mathbb R^{4d}:v+w=v'+w',\ |v|^2+|w|^2=|v'|^2+|w'|^2\},$$
with its relative Borel sigma-algebra. A collision measure is a nonnegative countably additive measure $\nu$ on this measurable space. It is symmetric if it is invariant under the exchanges $(v,w)\leftrightarrow(w,v)$, $(v',w')\leftrightarrow(w',v')$, and $(v,w)\leftrightarrow(v',w')$. These invariances are hypotheses on $\nu$, not consequences of energy and momentum conservation.

For a positive function $f:\mathbb R^d\to(0,\infty)$, write $Q(f)$ for a collision operator when the following **weak collision identity** holds for each test function $\varphi$ used:
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\varphi(v)Q(f)(v)\,dv=\frac14\int_{Q_{\rm el}}(f(v')f(w')-f(v)f(w))(\varphi(v)+\varphi(w)-\varphi(v')-\varphi(w'))\,d\nu,$$
with absolute convergence. This identity is the adopted mathematical collision model. Molecular chaos or a microscopic derivation of it is not part of the definition.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: For a fixed time, write $\ell=\log(f/f_{\rm ref})$. By [F3]–[F4], dominated differentiation gives $$\frac{dH}{dt}=\int_\Omega\int_{\mathbb R^d}(1+\ell)\,\partial_t f\,dv\,dr.$$ Substitute the transport equation. The spatial contribution is $$-\int_\Omega\int_{\mathbb R^d}(1+\ell)\,v\cdot\nabla_r f\,dv\,dr =-\int_\Omega\int_{\mathbb R^d}v\cdot\nabla_r(f\ell)\,dv\,dr.$$ For each fixed $v$, the integral of each coordinate derivative over the periodic rectangle is zero by the one-dimensional fundamental theorem of calculus and opposite-face identification; absolute integrability in [A2] permits Fubini [F2]. Thus the transport contribution vanishes.

The weak identity with test $1$ has zero bracket on every elastic collision, so $\int Q(f)\,dv=0$ at each $r,t$. Consequently the collision contribution from $(1+\ell)Q(f)$ equals that from $\ell Q(f)$. Apply the weak identity with $\varphi=\ell(r,\cdot,t)$ at fixed $(r,t)$. Since $f_{m ref}$ is constant, the sum $\ell(v)+\ell(w)-\ell(v')-\ell(w')$ is $\log(A/B)$. Hence $$\int \ell(v)Q(f)(v)\,dv= rac14\int_{Q_{m el}}(B-A)\log(A/B)\,d
u.$$ The velocity-side function is measurable in $(r,v)$ because $Q(f)=\partial_t f+v\cdot
abla_r f$ and $f>0$ have the stated regularity. Integration of its positive and negative parts over the sigma-finite Lebesgue velocity factor gives a measurable function of $r$; the weak identity makes that function equal to the collision integral at each $(r,t)$. By [A2] this collision integral is in $L^1(\Omega,dr)$, so integrate the identity in $r$ to obtain the asserted derivative formula. no collision/spatial product measure or interchange of $
u$ with spatial Lebesgue measure is used.

For positive $A,B$, strict increase of $\log$ [F5] makes $(A-B)\log(A/B)\ge0$, with equality exactly when $A=B$. The derivative in step 2.1 is therefore nonpositive. Let $g(r)$ be the nonnegative inner collision integral; it is measurable and integrable by [A2] and step 2.1. If $\int_\Omega g(r)\,dr=0$, then $g(r)=0$ for Lebesgue-almost every $r$. For each such $r$, a nonnegative function with zero $
u$-integral vanishes $
u$-almost everywhere: its sets where the value is at least $1/n$ all have $
u$-measure zero, and their countable union contains its positive set. This argument holds for an arbitrary measure, with no sigma-finiteness hypothesis. Thus $A=B$ for $
u$-almost every collision at almost every $r$. The converse follows by substitution in the derivative identity.

Under [A3], fix an $r$ for which collision balance holds $\nu$-almost everywhere. The function $(v,w,v',w')\mapsto A-B$ is continuous. If it were nonzero at an allowed collision, it would remain nonzero on a relative open neighborhood; full support of $\nu$ gives that neighborhood positive measure, contradicting balance. Hence balance holds for every elastic collision. The set of such $r$ has full Lebesgue measure and is dense in $\Omega$; continuity in $r$ extends the identity to any limit point when needed. [A1, A3, F1, step 3.1, algebra]

Fix such an $r$ and put $g(v)=\log(f(r,v,t)/f_{\rm ref})$. For any $a,u\in\mathbb R^d$ and any orthogonal rotation $R$, the pairs $(a+u,a-u)$ and $(a+Ru,a-Ru)$ have the same total momentum $2a$ and total squared speed $2|a|^2+2|u|^2$. Step 4.1 therefore gives $$g(a+u)+g(a-u)=g(a+Ru)+g(a-Ru).$$ For unit vectors $\theta,\eta$, put $u=s\theta$ and $R\theta=\eta$. The second-order Taylor expansion at $a$ gives $$g(a+s\theta)+g(a-s\theta)=2g(a)+s^2\theta^\top D^2g(a)\theta+o(s^2).$$ Equating the expansion for $\eta$, dividing by $s^2$ and sending $s\to0$ shows that the quadratic form of the symmetric Hessian is constant on the unit sphere. Testing coordinate vectors makes all diagonal entries equal; testing $(e_i+e_j)/\sqrt2$ makes each off-diagonal entry zero. Thus $D^2g(a)=\lambda(a)I$. [A1, A3, step 4.1, algebra]

Since $\partial_{ij}g=0$ for $i\ne j$, the fundamental theorem of calculus along coordinate segments shows $\partial_i g(v)$ depends only on $v_i$. Write it as $G_i(v_i)$. The diagonal Hessian equalities give $G_i'(v_i)=G_j'(v_j)$ for every pair of independent real coordinates $v_i,v_j$. Because $d\ge2$, varying these coordinates independently forces all these derivatives to be one constant $\lambda$. Integrating each first derivative gives $g(v)=\alpha+b\cdot v+\lambda|v|^2/2$. [A1, step 5.1, algebra]

If $\lambda>0$, $e^{g(v)}$ grows quadratically in every sufficiently large direction and is not integrable. If $\lambda=0$, $e^{\alpha+b\cdot v}$ is constant when $b=0$ and grows on a half-line when $b\ne0$, so it is not integrable over $\mathbb R^d$. Thus integrability forces $\lambda<0$. Completing the square writes $f(r,v,t)=C(r,t)\exp[-c(r,t)|v-u(r,t)|^2]$ for $C,c>0$, the Maxwellian velocity form. Conversely, when $g=\alpha+b\cdot v+\lambda|v|^2/2$, the sum $g(v)+g(w)$ is unchanged by every collision because total momentum and total squared speed are conserved; hence $A=B$ and the production is zero. This equality branch concerns the collision term only; a spatially varying Maxwellian may still evolve under transport. [A1, A3, F1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

Fix $d\ge2$. The **elastic collision set** is
$$Q_{\rm el}:=\{(v,w,v',w')\in\mathbb R^{4d}:v+w=v'+w',\ |v|^2+|w|^2=|v'|^2+|w'|^2\},$$
with its relative Borel sigma-algebra. A collision measure is a nonnegative countably additive measure $\nu$ on this measurable space. It is symmetric if it is invariant under the exchanges $(v,w)\leftrightarrow(w,v)$, $(v',w')\leftrightarrow(w',v')$, and $(v,w)\leftrightarrow(v',w')$. These invariances are hypotheses on $\nu$, not consequences of energy and momentum conservation.

For a positive function $f:\mathbb R^d\to(0,\infty)$, write $Q(f)$ for a collision operator when the following **weak collision identity** holds for each test function $\varphi$ used:
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\varphi(v)Q(f)(v)\,dv=\frac14\int_{Q_{\rm el}}(f(v')f(w')-f(v)f(w))(\varphi(v)+\varphi(w)-\varphi(v')-\varphi(w'))\,d\nu,$$
with absolute convergence. This identity is the adopted mathematical collision model. Molecular chaos or a microscopic derivation of it is not part of the definition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $O\subset\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge2$, be open, let $H\in C^2(O,\mathbb R)$, and let $J\subset\mathbb R$ be open. An energy $E\in J$ is **regular** if $\nabla H(x)\ne0$ for every $x\in\Sigma_E:=H^{-1}(\{E\})$. By the implicit-function theorem, a neighborhood of each point of a nonempty regular level is a graph $x_i=h(z)$.

In a graph chart, use the local area density $\sqrt{1+|\nabla h(z)|^2}\,dz$, where $dz$ is $(m-1)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. A **graph partition** on $\Sigma_E$ is a locally finite graph-chart cover with nonnegative smooth functions $\chi_a$ supported in their respective charts and summing to one on the level. Whenever such a partition is supplied, define the candidate weighted shell integral by
$$\mu_E(g):=\sum_a\int g(z,h_a(z))\chi_a(z,h_a(z))|\partial_iH(z,h_a(z))|^{-1}\,dz$$
for nonnegative Borel $g$. Its independence from the chosen chart partition, and its equality with $\int_{\Sigma_E}g|\nabla H|^{-1}dA_E$, are proved in the theorem on this page. If $0<\mu_E(1)<\infty$, the **microcanonical shell probability** is $\widehat\mu_E:=\mu_E/\mu_E(1)$.

This is an explicit chart-based definition, not a formal delta distribution $\delta(H-E)$. Critical levels are excluded.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n}$ be open, and let
$F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$.  Suppose $(a,b)\in U$, $F(a,b)=0$, and the
**partial derivative in the second block**

$$D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad D_yF(a,b)v:=DF(a,b)(0,v),$$

is invertible.  Put similarly $D_xF(a,b)u:=DF(a,b)(u,0)$.  Then there are open
neighbourhoods $P$ of $a$ and $Q$ of $b$, and a unique $C^1$ map
$\varphi:P\to Q$, such that

$$F(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x)\qquad((x,y)\in P\times Q).$$

After shrinking $P,Q$ if necessary, $D_yF(x,\varphi(x))$ is invertible and

$$D\varphi(x)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x))^{-1}D_xF(x,\varphi(x)).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $A \subseteq X$ be
nonempty and let $x, y \in X$. Then

$$|d(x,A) - d(y,A)| \le d(x,y),$$

with $d(\cdot,A)$ the distance to a nonempty set ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
Thus the real-valued function $u \mapsto d(u,A)$ changes by at most $d(u,v)$
between $u$ and $v$: it is **$1$-Lipschitz**.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $A \subseteq X$,
with closure, derived set and limit points as in
[[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]. Then:

1. If $A \ne \emptyset$, then $\overline{A} = \{\, x \in X : d(x,A) = 0 \,\}$,
   where $d(x,A)$ is the distance from a point to a nonempty set
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
2. $\overline{A} = A \cup A'$.
3. $\overline{A}$ is closed, contains $A$, and is contained in every closed
   $F \subseteq X$ with $A \subseteq F$. So $\overline{A}$ is the smallest closed
   superset of $A$, and $A$ is closed if and only if $A = \overline{A}$.

Claims 2 and 3 hold for every $A$, the empty set included: $\overline{\emptyset}$
is empty because no ball meets $\emptyset$, and $\emptyset$ is closed because $X$
is open ([[def-metric-topology]]). Claim 1 carries the hypothesis $A \ne \emptyset$
because $d(x,A)$ is defined only for nonempty $A$
([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

derivations.claim: Let $C$ be a compact energy band containing the support of $f$. At each $x\in H^{-1}(C)$, some coordinate derivative $\partial_iH(x)$ is nonzero. By [F2] a neighborhood is parameterized by the remaining coordinates $z$ and energy $E$, with $x_i=h(z,E)$. Compactness gives a finite cover by such charts. Refine the cover by finitely many balls whose closures lie in chart domains and whose smaller concentric balls cover $H^{-1}(C)$. Choose standard smooth bump functions $\psi_a$ supported in the larger balls and positive on the smaller balls, and let $\Psi=\sum_a\psi_a$. Its minimum on $H^{-1}(C)$ is positive. Choose a smooth scalar cutoff $\eta$ that is zero below one quarter of this minimum and one above one half of it. Then $\chi_a=\eta(\Psi)\psi_a/\Psi$, extended by zero where $\Psi=0$, is smooth, supported in its chart, and the sum is one near $H^{-1}(C)$.

At the stated $C^2$ regularity, $X_H$ in [F5] has continuous first derivatives. Along every flow curve, $\frac{d}{ds}H(\phi_s(x))=\sum_j(H_{q_j}H_{p_j}-H_{p_j}H_{q_j})(\phi_s(x))=0$. Differentiating its integral equation $\phi_s(x)=x+\int_0^sX_H(\phi_u(x))\,du$ in $x$ gives $J_s=I+\int_0^sDX_H(\phi_u(x))J_u\,du$, where $J_s=D_x\phi_s(x)$; on each compact flow segment the $C^1$ derivatives are continuous, so difference quotients pass through this finite integral. Thus $\partial_sJ_s=DX_H(\phi_s(x))J_s$. Differentiating the determinant by multilinearity in its columns gives $\partial_s\det J_s=(\operatorname{tr}DX_H)(\phi_s(x))\det J_s$. Indeed $J_s$ is invertible by the inverse flow, and the sum of determinants with one column replaced by $DX_H$ times that column is $\det J_s\,\operatorname{tr}(J_s^{-1}DX_HJ_s)=\det J_s\,\operatorname{tr}DX_H$. Equality of the continuous mixed second derivatives of $H$ gives $\operatorname{tr}DX_H=\sum_j(\partial_{q_j}\partial_{p_j}H-\partial_{p_j}\partial_{q_j}H)=0$. Since $\det J_0=1$, $\det J_s=1$ throughout the flow domain; [F3] then gives Lebesgue-volume preservation. Both invariances therefore hold for the entire $C^2$ scope of this item.

In each chart, the map $(z,E)\mapsto(z,h_a(z,E))$ is injective after shrinking the chart, and its absolute Jacobian is $|\partial_Eh_a|=|\partial_iH|^{-1}$. By [F3] and Tonelli [F4], $$\int_O f(x)\chi_a(x)\,dx =\int_J\int f(z,h_a(z,E))\chi_a(z,h_a(z,E))|\partial_iH|^{-1}\,dz\,dE.$$ Implicit differentiation gives $\partial_{z_j}h_a=-\partial_jH/\partial_iH$, so the graph area density is $$\sqrt{1+|\nabla_zh_a|^2}\,dz=\frac{|\nabla H|}{|\partial_iH|}\,dz.$$ The inner integral is therefore the corresponding chart contribution to the candidate $\mu_E(f)$ in [F1]. Sum the finitely many charts and use $\sum_a\chi_a=1$ on the support to obtain the asserted coarea identity.

On overlaps, if one graph parameterization is obtained from another by a $C^1$ coordinate change $\psi$, its Gram matrix is transformed by $G\mapsto(D\psi)^	op G(D\psi)$. Taking determinants shows the area density changes by $|\det D\psi|$, exactly the ordinary chart Jacobian. Implicit differentiation gives $\sqrt{1+|
abla h|^2}/|
abla H|=|\partial_iH|^{-1}$, so the chart contributions define the same measure independent of the partition and equal $\int_{\Sigma_E}g|
abla H|^{-1}dA_E$. Each shell is a closed subset of compact $H^{-1}(\{E\})$, hence compact. A finite collection of graph charts with $
abla H$ bounded away from zero on that compact level gives finite area and hence $\mu_E(1)<\infty$. If the shell is nonempty, one graph chart contains an open patch; its coordinate domain has positive $(2n-1)$-dimensional measure and the continuous density $|
abla H|^{-1}dA_E/dz$ is positive there, so $\mu_E(1)>0$.

Fix a compact band and a compactly supported continuous test $g$ on it. For a continuous compactly supported scalar function $q$ on $J$, the coarea identity from step 2.1 and the Hamiltonian volume/energy invariance from step 1.2 give $$\int_Jq(E)\mu_E(g\circ\phi_t)\,dE =\int_Oq(H(x))g(\phi_tx)\,dx =\int_Oq(H(x))g(x)\,dx =\int_Jq(E)\mu_E(g)\,dE.$$ The second equality is the change of variables by the volume-preserving diffeomorphism $\phi_t$; $H\circ\phi_t=H$ keeps the energy weight fixed. For each test $g$, both functions of $E$ in the outer integrals are continuous locally: use the finite chart representation in step 2.1, compact chart support, the positive lower bound for $|\nabla H|$, and dominated convergence [F6]. Their difference integrates to zero against every compactly supported continuous $q$. If the continuous difference were nonzero at one energy, it would keep one strict sign on a neighborhood; a nonnegative continuous bump $q$ supported there would make the integral nonzero. Thus $\mu_E(g\circ\phi_t)=\mu_E(g)$ for every $E$ in the band.

Fix a closed subset $F$ of a nonempty shell. If $F=\varnothing$, both measures assign it zero. Otherwise let $\chi$ be a continuous compactly supported cutoff equal to one on the compact shell; the same finite-ball bump construction used in 1.1 supplies it. In the ambient band set $g_n(x)=\chi(x)\max\{0,1-n\,\operatorname{dist}(x,F)\}$. By [F7], $g_n$ is continuous, $0\le g_n\le1$, and its restriction to $\Sigma_E$ converges pointwise to $\mathbf1_F$. Because $\phi_t$ maps the shell onto itself, $g_n\circ\phi_t$ converges there to $\mathbf1_{\phi_t^{-1}F}$. Apply step 3.1 to each $g_n$ and use dominated convergence [F6] for the finite shell measure from step 2.2; this gives $\mu_E(\phi_t^{-1}F)=\mu_E(F)$ for every closed $F\subseteq\Sigma_E$. Closed sets form a pi-system generating the shell Borel sigma-algebra, and both $\mu_E$ and its pushforward have the same finite total mass because $\phi_t$ maps the shell onto itself.

By [F8], agreement on closed sets and equality of total masses imply that $\mu_E$ equals its pushforward on every Borel subset of $\Sigma_E$. Divide by $0<\mu_E(1)<\infty$ from step 2.2. Hence the normalized regular-shell probability is invariant for each such $E$, not merely almost every energy.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $O\subset\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge2$, be open, let $H\in C^2(O,\mathbb R)$, and let $J\subset\mathbb R$ be open. An energy $E\in J$ is **regular** if $\nabla H(x)\ne0$ for every $x\in\Sigma_E:=H^{-1}(\{E\})$. By the implicit-function theorem, a neighborhood of each point of a nonempty regular level is a graph $x_i=h(z)$.

In a graph chart, use the local area density $\sqrt{1+|\nabla h(z)|^2}\,dz$, where $dz$ is $(m-1)$-dimensional Lebesgue measure. A **graph partition** on $\Sigma_E$ is a locally finite graph-chart cover with nonnegative smooth functions $\chi_a$ supported in their respective charts and summing to one on the level. Whenever such a partition is supplied, define the candidate weighted shell integral by
$$\mu_E(g):=\sum_a\int g(z,h_a(z))\chi_a(z,h_a(z))|\partial_iH(z,h_a(z))|^{-1}\,dz$$
for nonnegative Borel $g$. Its independence from the chosen chart partition, and its equality with $\int_{\Sigma_E}g|\nabla H|^{-1}dA_E$, are proved in the theorem on this page. If $0<\mu_E(1)<\infty$, the **microcanonical shell probability** is $\widehat\mu_E:=\mu_E/\mu_E(1)$.

This is an explicit chart-based definition, not a formal delta distribution $\delta(H-E)$. Critical levels are excluded.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n}$ be open, and let
$F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$.  Suppose $(a,b)\in U$, $F(a,b)=0$, and the
**partial derivative in the second block**

$$D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad D_yF(a,b)v:=DF(a,b)(0,v),$$

is invertible.  Put similarly $D_xF(a,b)u:=DF(a,b)(u,0)$.  Then there are open
neighbourhoods $P$ of $a$ and $Q$ of $b$, and a unique $C^1$ map
$\varphi:P\to Q$, such that

$$F(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x)\qquad((x,y)\in P\times Q).$$

After shrinking $P,Q$ if necessary, $D_yF(x,\varphi(x))$ is invertible and

$$D\varphi(x)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x))^{-1}D_xF(x,\varphi(x)).$$

spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $A \subseteq X$ be
nonempty and let $x, y \in X$. Then

$$|d(x,A) - d(y,A)| \le d(x,y),$$

between $u$ and $v$: it is **$1$-Lipschitz**.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $A$ be self-adjoint with regular Borel projection-valued measure $E$ from [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], with $E((-\infty,a))=0$ for finite $a\in\mathbb R$. For each $\gamma>0$, define the bounded Gibbs operator $K_\gamma:=\Phi_E(f_\gamma)$ using the bounded Borel PVM integral of [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], where $f_\gamma(\lambda)=e^{-\gamma\lambda}$ for $\lambda\ge a$ and $f_\gamma(\lambda)=e^{-\gamma a}$ for $\lambda<a$. Fix $\beta>0$ and suppose $K_\beta$ is trace class in the sense of [[def-trace-class-operator]]. Then $K_\beta$ is injective and has a finite or countable orthonormal basis $(u_j)$ of $\mathcal H$ with $Au_j=E_ju_j$, $E_j\ge a$, and $K_\beta u_j=e^{-\beta E_j}u_j$. Its partition function $Z_\beta:=\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta=\sum_j e^{-\beta E_j}$ is positive and finite, and $\rho_\beta:=K_\beta/Z_\beta$ is positive with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_\beta=1$. For every $B\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta B)=\sum_j(e^{-\beta E_j}/Z_\beta)\langle Bu_j,u_j\rangle$ absolutely. Further, let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and suppose that for every compact $C\subset J$ there is a summable family $a_j\ge0$ with $(1+|E_j|^2)e^{-\gamma E_j}\le a_j$ for all $j$ and $\gamma\in C$. Then for each $\gamma\in J$, $K_\gamma$ is trace class with partition function $Z_\gamma:=\operatorname{Tr}K_\gamma=\sum_j e^{-\gamma E_j}$. With $p_j(\gamma):=e^{-\gamma E_j}/Z_\gamma$, define $\bar E_\gamma:=\sum_jp_j(\gamma)E_j$, $\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(E):=\sum_jp_j(\gamma)(E_j-\bar E_\gamma)^2$, and $S_\gamma:=-\sum_jp_j(\gamma)\log p_j(\gamma)$. These quantities are finite and satisfy $-\partial_\gamma\log Z_\gamma=\bar E_\gamma$, $\partial_\gamma^2\log Z_\gamma=\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(E)$, and $S_\gamma=\log Z_\gamma+\gamma\bar E_\gamma$ as in [[thm-tdmath-summable-canonical-differentiation]]. Countable nonnegative sums use the finite-subsum supremum convention of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a separable complex Hilbert space, let
$T\in\mathcal S_1(H)$ be trace class, and let $(P_n)_{n\ge1}$ be any supplied sequence of
finite-rank orthogonal projections on $H$ such that $P_n\to I$ strongly. Then
$$\|P_nTP_n-T\|_1\longrightarrow0.$$
The projections need not be increasing. For example, the initial projections
onto the first $n$ vectors of a supplied countable orthonormal basis satisfy
the hypothesis.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a **self-adjoint positive** trace-class operator
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every
$x\in H$. Let $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ be the positive eigenvalues of
$T$ listed with multiplicity
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) and let
$(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ be the zero-padded singular-value sequence
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$
where the sum is over the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity and the
equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for
$n$ beyond the rank). This is the positive compact self-adjoint case only; it is
**not** Lidskii's theorem for arbitrary trace-class operators, which is not
claimed here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]) and let
$S\in\mathcal B(H)$ be bounded. Then $ST$ and $TS$ are trace class and
$$\operatorname{tr}(ST)=\operatorname{tr}(TS) .$$
If $A,B\in\mathcal B(H)$ are Hilbert–Schmidt relative to a supplied Hilbert
basis $E$ of $H$ ([[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]]), then the products $AB$ and
$BA$ are trace class and
$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

derivations.claim: Each multiplier $e^{-iE_jt/\hbar}$ has modulus one by [F6]. Thus $U_t$ preserves the norm of finite linear combinations of the complete orthonormal basis; it extends by density to an isometry on the Hilbert space. The similarly defined $U_{-t}$ is its inverse, so $U_t$ is unitary and depends continuously on $t$ on each finite-dimensional energy span. The arguments $E_jt/\hbar$ are dimensionless.

By [F2], $\rho_t=U_t\rho U_t^*$ is trace class. It is positive because $\langle\rho_t x,x\rangle=\langle\rho U_t^*x,U_t^*x\rangle\ge0$, and cyclicity [F5] gives $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_t=\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$.

Enumerate the distinct energy eigenspaces and let $P_N$ project onto the first $N$ of them, with $P_N=I$ after the list is exhausted if it is finite. Their union spans the eigenbasis, so $P_N\to I$ strongly. The Hilbert space is separable by the countable complete basis in [A1]. Therefore [F3] gives $\|P_N\rho P_N-\rho\|_1\to0$. Unitary invariance of trace norm follows from [F2] in both directions: $\|U_tRU_t^*\|_1\le\|R\|_1$ and $R=U_t^*(U_tRU_t^*)U_t$ gives the reverse inequality. Consequently $$\|U_tP_N\rho P_NU_t^*-\rho_t\|_1=\|P_N\rho P_N-\rho\|_1$$ uniformly in $t$.

For fixed $N$, the matrix of $U_tP_N\rho P_NU_t^*$ on its finite-dimensional range has continuous entries, hence is continuous in trace norm. Step 2.2 makes $\rho_t$ a uniform trace-norm limit on compact time intervals of these continuous maps; therefore $t\mapsto\rho_t$ is trace-norm continuous. On $[0,T]$ it is uniformly continuous. Riemann sums for a uniformly continuous Banach-valued function are Cauchy: two sums are compared on a common refinement and their difference is bounded by $T$ times the modulus of continuity at the larger mesh. Completeness in [F2] supplies the trace-class integral and its usual norm bound.

In the eigenbasis, the $(i,j)$ matrix entry of $U_tP_N\rho P_NU_t^*$ is $\langle\rho u_j,u_i\rangle e^{i(E_j-E_i)t/\hbar}$. Its time-average factor is $1$ if $E_i=E_j$; if $E_i\ne E_j$, direct integration using [F6] gives absolute value at most $2\hbar/(T|E_j-E_i|)$, which tends to zero. Since the compression is finite dimensional, entrywise convergence implies trace-norm convergence. Hence the finite compressed average tends to $\sum_{E\text{ among the first }N}P_E\rho P_E$.

Each block $P_E\rho P_E$ is positive trace class. The sum of their traces is $$\sum_E\sum_{u_j\in\operatorname{ran}P_E}\langle\rho u_j,u_j\rangle =\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$$ by [F4] and the complete basis in [A1]. Therefore their finite partial sums are Cauchy in trace norm: for a positive finite block tail its trace norm equals its trace, and the scalar trace tail tends to zero. Their limit $\rho_{\rm diag}$ exists in trace norm, is positive, and has trace one.

Given $\epsilon>0$, choose $N$ so the compression error in step 2.2 and the diagonal tail in step 5.1 are each below $\epsilon/3$. The norm bound for the Riemann integral in step 3.1 makes the average of the compression error at most $\epsilon/3$, uniformly in $T$. For this fixed $N$, step 4.1 makes the finite compressed average differ from its finite diagonal limit by less than $\epsilon/3$ for all sufficiently large $T$. The triangle inequality then gives $\|\bar\rho_T-\rho_{\rm diag}\|_1<\epsilon$.

For bounded observable $B$, the trace-class ideal and trace estimates in [F2] and [F4] give $|\operatorname{Tr}((\bar\rho_T-\rho_{\rm diag})B)|\le\|\bar\rho_T-\rho_{\rm diag}\|_1\|B\|$. Step 6.1 sends the right-hand side to zero. The conclusion is only convergence of time-averaged states in the stated trace norm.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and let $A$ be self-adjoint with regular Borel projection-valued measure $E$ from [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], with $E((-\infty,a))=0$ for finite $a\in\mathbb R$. For each $\gamma>0$, define the bounded Gibbs operator $K_\gamma:=\Phi_E(f_\gamma)$ using the bounded Borel PVM integral of [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]], where $f_\gamma(\lambda)=e^{-\gamma\lambda}$ for $\lambda\ge a$ and $f_\gamma(\lambda)=e^{-\gamma a}$ for $\lambda<a$. Fix $\beta>0$ and suppose $K_\beta$ is trace class in the sense of [[def-trace-class-operator]]. Then $K_\beta$ is injective and has a finite or countable orthonormal basis $(u_j)$ of $\mathcal H$ with $Au_j=E_ju_j$, $E_j\ge a$, and $K_\beta u_j=e^{-\beta E_j}u_j$. Its partition function $Z_\beta:=\operatorname{Tr}K_\beta=\sum_j e^{-\beta E_j}$ is positive and finite, and $\rho_\beta:=K_\beta/Z_\beta$ is positive with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_\beta=1$. For every $B\in\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\beta B)=\sum_j(e^{-\beta E_j}/Z_\beta)\langle Bu_j,u_j\rangle$ absolutely. Further, let $J\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and suppose that for every compact $C\subset J$ there is a summable family $a_j\ge0$ with $(1+|E_j|^2)e^{-\gamma E_j}\le a_j$ for all $j$ and $\gamma\in C$. Then for each $\gamma\in J$, $K_\gamma$ is trace class with partition function $Z_\gamma:=\operatorname{Tr}K_\gamma=\sum_j e^{-\gamma E_j}$. With $p_j(\gamma):=e^{-\gamma E_j}/Z_\gamma$, define $\bar E_\gamma:=\sum_jp_j(\gamma)E_j$, $\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(E):=\sum_jp_j(\gamma)(E_j-\bar E_\gamma)^2$, and $S_\gamma:=-\sum_jp_j(\gamma)\log p_j(\gamma)$. These quantities are finite and satisfy $-\partial_\gamma\log Z_\gamma=\bar E_\gamma$, $\partial_\gamma^2\log Z_\gamma=\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(E)$, and $S_\gamma=\log Z_\gamma+\gamma\bar E_\gamma$ as in [[thm-tdmath-summable-canonical-differentiation]]. Countable nonnegative sums use the finite-subsum supremum convention of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]].

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $K$ be a nonempty compact subset of $\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, with its Borel sigma-algebra, and let $a:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. The **convex hull** $\operatorname{conv}K$ is the set of finite convex combinations of points of $K$. A **phase generator** is a point $y\in K$ with declared energy $a(y)$. A **mixture** is a Borel probability measure $P$ on $K$. Its barycenter and mean energy are the coordinatewise Lebesgue integrals
$$\bar y(P):=\int_K y\,dP(y)\in\mathbb R^d,\qquad \bar a(P):=\int_K a(y)\,dP(y)\in\mathbb R.$$
These integrals are finite because each coordinate and $a$ are bounded on compact $K$. For prescribed mean $x\in\operatorname{conv}K$, the **mixture energy** is
$$a_{\rm mix}(x):=\inf\{\bar a(P):P\text{ is a Borel probability on }K,\ \bar y(P)=x\}.$$
The admissible set is nonempty since every finite convex combination of points of $K$ is the barycenter of a finite atomic probability. The definition does not assert that the infimum is attained; the theorem on this page gives a compact continuous sufficient condition.

Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty compact, $d\ge1$, and $a:K\to\mathbb R$ continuous. Define $a_{\rm mix}$ as in [[def-tdmath-mixture-generator-space-and-energy]]. Then for every $x\in\operatorname{conv}K$ the infimum defining $a_{\rm mix}(x)$ is attained by a Borel probability measure supported on at most $d+1$ points. The function $a_{\rm mix}$ is lower semicontinuous and convex on $\operatorname{conv}K$, and is the greatest convex function on $\operatorname{conv}K$ bounded above by $a$ on $K$. Minimizing over all Borel probabilities on $K$ gives the same attained value as minimizing over finite mixtures. This is a mathematical compactness result; it makes no phase-preparation or equilibrium postulate.

derivations.claim: For each integer $n\ge2$, the set $E_n=[1/n,1)$ is Borel, and $\bigcup_{n\ge2}E_n=(0,1)$. Since $P((0,1))=1$, countable subadditivity implies $P(E_n)>0$ for at least one $n$; otherwise the union would have probability zero. On $E_n$, $x\ge1/n$, while elsewhere $x\ge0$, so $$\int_{(0,1)}x\,dP\ge \frac1nP(E_n)>0.$$ Therefore every admissible probability has strictly positive objective. [A1, F1, algebra]

The point mass $\delta_{1/n}$ at $1/n$ is a Borel probability on $(0,1)$ and has objective $1/n$. These values tend to zero, while 1.1 shows all objectives are positive. Hence the infimum is zero and is not attained. The generator set is noncompact, so this conclusion does not contradict the compact result [F2]; it shows why an attainment theorem must retain its compactness/coercivity hypotheses. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

derivations.claim: Since $e_{N,k}\ge1$, $e^{Ne_{N,k}^2}\ge e^N$. For $x\ge e^N$, $x-1\le\lfloor x\rfloor\le x$, so $$e_{N,k}^2+\frac1N\log(1-e^{-N})\le \frac1N\log g_{N,k}\le e_{N,k}^2.$$ The error tends to zero uniformly in $k$. The grid mesh is $1/N$; for a continuous function on $[1,2]$, uniform continuity makes its grid maxima converge to its interval maximum.

Let $Z_N(b)=\sum_{k=0}^Ng_{N,k}e^{-Nb e_{N,k}}$ and $m_N=\max_k[N^{-1}\log g_{N,k}-b e_{N,k}]$. The largest summand is $e^{Nm_N}$ and there are $N+1$ summands, so $$m_N\le N^{-1}\log Z_N(b)\le m_N+N^{-1}\log(N+1).$$ By 1.1, $m_N\to\max_{e\in[1,2]}(e^2-be)$. If $e=\theta\cdot1+(1-\theta)\cdot2$ with $0<\theta<1$, direct expansion gives $$e^2-be=\theta(1-b)+(1-\theta)(4-2b)-\theta(1-\theta),$$ strictly below the weighted endpoint values. Thus the maximum is at an endpoint and equals $\max(1-b,4-2b)$.

If $K=\emptyset$, the probability is zero. Otherwise, for compact $K\subset(1,2)$ strict convexity gives $$\eta:=\min_{e\in K}\left[\max(1-b,4-2b)-(e^2-be)\right]>0$$ by [F3]. Uniform approximation in 1.1 makes every grid exponent in $K$ at most the maximum minus $\eta/2$ for all sufficiently large $N$. On the other hand, an endpoint group has exponent tending to the maximum. By [F2], $\log(N+1)/N\le2\sqrt{N+1}/N\to0$, so the polynomial factor is dominated by the exponential gap and the canonical probability of $K$, at most $(N+1)e^{-N\eta/2+o(N)}$, tends to zero.

Choose integers $k_N$ with $e_{N,k_N}\to e\in(1,2)$. The microcanonical exact-group law has energy density exactly $e_{N,k_N}$ at every state. By 1.1 its entropy density $N^{-1}\log g_{N,k_N}$ tends to $e^2$. Thus, for example at the crossing $b=3$, canonical mass escapes every compact neighborhood of any interior target while the microcanonical group remains there. Finally $s(3/2)=9/4<5/2=(s(1)+s(2))/2$, so $s(e)=e^2$ is not concave. The example is a constructed model, not an observation about a material.

citations.quote:
A **symplectic form** on a smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth two-form $\omega$
such that

1. $d\omega=0$, and
2. $(T_pM,\omega_p)$ is a [[def-symplectic-vector-space|symplectic vector
   space]] for every $p\in M$.

The pair $(M,\omega)$ is a **symplectic manifold**. Thus both closedness and
pointwise nondegeneracy are required. A zero-dimensional manifold with its
zero two-form satisfies the definition.

For $H\in C^\infty(M)$, its **Hamiltonian vector field** is the vector field
$X_H$ determined by the library sign convention

$$\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH.$$

A vector field $X$ is **Hamiltonian** if $\iota_X\omega=dH$ for some smooth
function $H$; such an $H$ is a **Hamiltonian function for $X$**. A function and
its vector field are distinct data, and completeness of $X_H$ is not assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(M,\omega)$ be a smooth $2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold and $H\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, with Hamiltonian field defined by $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$. Wherever its local flow $\phi_t$ is defined, it preserves the symplectic form and the volume measure $m$ determined by $\omega^n/n!$. No completeness is asserted. Let $R$ be a measurable region invariant under a nonzero-time map $T=\phi_\tau$, so $T$ restricts to a self-map $R\to R$; then this restriction preserves the volume measure $m|_R$. If $m(R)<\infty$, then for every measurable $E\subseteq R$, almost every point of $E$ returns to $E$ infinitely often under forward iteration.

If $m(R)=1$ and $T$ is ergodic, then for every $f\in L^1(R,m)$ the averages $N^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}f(T^jx)$ converge almost everywhere and in $L^1$ to $\int_Rf\,dm$. Without ergodicity, the limit is the invariant conditional expectation supplied by Birkhoff's theorem, not necessarily the space mean. Finally, if each stated time map $\phi_t$ is a diffeomorphism of a finite invariant region $R$, a density $p_0\ge0$ with $\int_Rp_0\,dm=1$ and $\int_R|p_0\log p_0|\,dm<\infty$ transports by $p_t=p_0\circ\phi_{-t}$ with conserved fine-grained entropy $-k_B\int_Rp_t\log p_t\,dm$, using $0\log0=0$. Volume preservation alone does not imply ergodicity or a time-average/ensemble identity.

A measure-preserving system is **ergodic for $\mu$** if each $E\in\mathcal I$ has $\mu(E)=0$ or $\mu(X\setminus E)=0$, with $\mathcal I$ as in [[def-strict-and-mod-null-invariant-sigma-algebras]]. For a probability system this means $\mu(E)\in\{0,1\}$. The definition is relative to the invariant measure; no probability assumption is implicit in the general null/conull formulation.

derivations.claim: Write $X_H=a\partial_q+b\partial_p$. Then $\iota_{X_H}(dq\wedge dp)=a\,dp-b\,dq$, while $dH=-\sin q\,dq$. Equating coefficients gives $a=0$ and $b=\sin q$. The explicit solution is $$\phi_t(q,p)=(q,p+t\sin q\pmod{2\pi}),$$ which is defined for every real $t$ and is a diffeomorphism with inverse $\phi_{-t}$.

Since $H\circ\phi_t=H$, the set $A$ is invariant under every $\phi_t$. The torus has total area $(2\pi)^2=4\pi^2$. The allowed $q$ values in $A$ have total length $\pi$, while $p$ ranges over length $2\pi$, so $m(A)=2\pi^2$, strictly between zero and total area. The map preserves area by [F2], and the invariant set violates the criterion [F3]; hence it is not ergodic for any nonzero sampling time.
