citations.quote: For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

derivations.claim: The unitary evolution sends $\psi$ to $(e^{-iE_1t/\hbar}u_1+e^{-iE_2t/\hbar}u_2)/\sqrt2$, which remains a unit vector by [F2]. Its rank-one density has eigenvalues $1,0$, so its entropy is $-k_B(1\log1+0\log0)=0$ for every $t$.

The two energy eigenspaces are one-dimensional. The matrix entry between them is an exponential with nonzero frequency; by [F1] its average has magnitude at most $\hbar/(T|E_1-E_2|)$ and tends to zero. The diagonal entries remain $1/2$, so the direct finite-dimensional average yields $\rho_{\rm diag}=\tfrac12P_1+\tfrac12P_2$. Its eigenvalues are $(1/2,1/2)$, so $$S(\rho_{\rm diag})=-k_B\left(\tfrac12\log\tfrac12+\tfrac12\log\tfrac12\right)=k_B\log2.$$ Since every $S(\rho_t)=0$, the time average of instantaneous entropy is exactly zero.

In the basis $(u_1,u_2)$, $\bar\rho_T$ has diagonal entries $1/2$ and off-diagonal entry $$c_T=\frac1{2T}\int_0^T e^{-i(E_1-E_2)t/\hbar}\,dt,$$ whose magnitude is at most $\hbar/(T|E_1-E_2|)$ by direct integration. Its eigenvalues are $1/2\pm|c_T|$, so both tend to $1/2$. Continuity of $x\mapsto-x\log x$ at $1/2$ gives $S(\bar\rho_T)\to k_B\log2$. Thus entropy of the averaged state has a nonzero limit even though the averaged instantaneous entropy remains zero.

case_scope.source_excerpt:
Take $\Omega$ to be a finite nonempty microstate set as in [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]: distinct elements count as distinct microstates, and the physical energy values are finite and measured in joules in the declared rest frame. For the physical internal-energy interpretation, use one declared fixed Galilean chart for every stage, with the bulk center-of-mass and separately tracked external-energy sectors suppressed from this finite protocol. The companion mechanical model supplies the center-of-mass data required by the microstate supplier; when the common chart is called a center-of-mass rest chart throughout the protocol, its center-of-mass velocity is constant over the modeled interval, and one constant boost selects that chart. This fixed-chart idealization does not infer a rest chart from the finite set or transition kernels, and does not describe an accelerating bulk body. Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and stage energy functions $E_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$ for $k=0,\ldots,m$, with the energy offsets fixed by the declared protocol model. Its undirected rate graph has an edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $\pi_iq_{ij}>0$; detailed balance makes this equivalent to $\pi_jq_{ji}>0$.

On a finite nonempty state set $S$, a discrete transition kernel is a matrix $K:S\times S\to[0,1]$ satisfying $\sum_{j\in S}K(i,j)=1$ for every $i\in S$. For a strictly positive row probability vector $\pi\in\Delta(S)$, the kernel satisfies $\pi$-detailed balance when $\pi_iK(i,j)=\pi_jK(j,i)$ for every $i,j\in S$. This identity pairs the supports of forward and reversed transitions. A rate model or a reversible kernel is a mathematical/physical model class; no observed trajectory is asserted by the definition.

A finite rate model consists of a finite nonempty state set $S$ and rates $q_{ij}\ge0$ in seconds$^{-1}$ for $i\ne j$. Set $q_{ii}=-\sum_{j\ne i}q_{ij}$. A row probability vector is $p=(p_i)_{i\in S}$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$; write $\Delta(S)=\{p\in[0,1]^S:\sum_i p_i=1\}$. A time-dependent law is a coordinatewise continuously differentiable map $p:[0,\infty)\to\Delta(S)$, with a right derivative at $t=0$, that satisfies the continuous-time master equation $\dot p_i(t)=\sum_{j\ne i}[p_j(t)q_{ji}-p_i(t)q_{ij}]$ for every $t\ge0$. The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: Put $c=1+\max_i\sum_{j\ne i}q_{ij}$ and $P=I+Q/c$, where $Q=(q_{ij})$. Then $P$ has nonnegative entries and row sums one. The series $p(t)=e^{-ct}\sum_{n=0}^\infty (ct)^n p(0)P^n/n!$ and its differentiated series converge uniformly on bounded time intervals; its coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one, so it is a probability vector, starts at $p(0)$, and differentiates to $\dot p=pQ$. Its $n=0$ term gives $p_i(t)\ge e^{-ct}p_i(0)>0$. For uniqueness, the difference $z$ of two solutions satisfies $z'=zQ$; with $C=\max_i\sum_j|q_{ij}|$ and $U(t)=\int_0^t\|z(s)\|_1ds$, one has $U'(t)=\|z(t)\|_1\le C U(t)$. Thus $(e^{-Ct}U(t))'\le0$ and $U(0)=0\le U(t)$ force $U=0$, hence $z=0$.

With $r_i=p_i/\pi_i$, detailed balance gives $\dot p_i=\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}(r_j-r_i)$. By [F4], differentiating the finite entropy sum gives $D'=\sum_i\dot p_i(\log r_i+1)=\sum_i\dot p_i\log r_i$, since $\sum_i\dot p_i=0$. Pairing the $i,j$ terms gives $D'=-\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}a_{ij}(r_i-r_j)(\log r_i-\log r_j)\le0$: if $r_i\ge r_j$, then $\log r_i-\log r_j=-\log(r_j/r_i)\ge0$ by [F3], and the reversed order gives the same product sign. The mean value theorem [F5] on each compact time interval makes $D$ nonincreasing.

Set $u_i=r_i-1$, so $\sum_i\pi_i u_i=0$, and $V(t)=\sum_i\pi_i u_i^2$. Since $\dot u_i=\pi_i^{-1}\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}(u_j-u_i)$, differentiating and pairing the two orientations of each edge gives $V'=2\sum_i u_i\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}(u_j-u_i)=-2\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}a_{ij}(u_i-u_j)^2$.

Let $a_*=\min_{\{i,j\}\in E}a_{ij}>0$. Fix a root state and choose one simple path from it to each state; this is only a finite family of choices, obtainable successively, and each path has length at most $N-1$. Telescoping and [F6] give $(u_i-u_r)^2\le(N-1)\sum_{\{j,k\}\in E}(u_j-u_k)^2$. The zero-mean identity gives $u_r=-\sum_i\pi_i(u_i-u_r)$; expanding $\sum_i\pi_i[(u_i-u_r)-\sum_j\pi_j(u_j-u_r)]^2\ge0$ yields $u_r^2\le\sum_i\pi_i(u_i-u_r)^2$. Since $(x+y)^2\le2x^2+2y^2$ and $\sum_i\pi_i=1$, it follows that $V\le4(N-1)\sum_E(u_i-u_j)^2\le4(N-1)a_*^{-1}\sum_Ea_{ij}(u_i-u_j)^2$.

Thus $V'\le-2\lambda V$ with $\lambda=a_*/[4(N-1)]>0$. By [F5], the derivative of $e^{2\lambda t}V(t)$ is nonpositive and that function is nonincreasing, so $V(t)\le e^{-2\lambda t}V(0)$. Since $\pi_i u_i(t)^2\le V(t)$ and $p_i-\pi_i=\pi_i u_i$, each $p_i(t)\to\pi_i$.

Take $\Omega$ to be a finite nonempty microstate set as in [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]: distinct elements count as distinct microstates, and the physical energy values are finite and measured in joules in the declared rest frame. For the physical internal-energy interpretation, use one declared fixed Galilean chart for every stage, with the bulk center-of-mass and separately tracked external-energy sectors suppressed from this finite protocol. The companion mechanical model supplies the center-of-mass data required by the microstate supplier; when the common chart is called a center-of-mass rest chart throughout the protocol, its center-of-mass velocity is constant over the modeled interval, and one constant boost selects that chart. This fixed-chart idealization does not infer a rest chart from the finite set or transition kernels, and does not describe an accelerating bulk body. Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and stage energy functions $E_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$ for $k=0,\ldots,m$, with the energy offsets fixed by the declared protocol model. Fix inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$. The finite partition sum and canonical probability vector at stage $k$ are $Z_k=\sum_{i\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E_k(i)}$ and $\pi_k(i)=e^{-\beta E_k(i)}/Z_k$. Since $\Omega$ is nonempty and finite and each energy is finite, $0<Z_k<\infty$ and $\pi_k$ is a strictly positive probability vector.

A transition kernel at stage $k$ is a matrix $K_k(i,j)\ge0$ with $\sum_{j\in\Omega}K_k(i,j)=1$. In the forward stage order, the energy changes instantaneously from $E_{k-1}$ to $E_k$ while the state is still $i_{k-1}$; the subsequent bath transition samples $i_k$ using $K_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$ at fixed energy $E_k$. A path is $\omega=(i_0,\ldots,i_m)\in\Omega^{m+1}$. The initial law is a probability vector $\mu_0:\Omega\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{i\in\Omega}\mu_0(i)=1$. Its path probability is $P_F(\omega)=\mu_0(i_0)\prod_{k=1}^mK_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$; summing over all paths gives $1$ by the normalization of $\mu_0$ and the row sums of the kernels.

Work on the system is positive when energy is supplied to it, and heat into the system is positive when a bath transition raises its energy. Define $W(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_{k-1})-E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})]$ and $Q_{\mathrm{in}}(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_k)-E_k(i_{k-1})]$, both in joules. Define $F_k=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_k$ and $\Delta F=F_m-F_0=-\beta^{-1}\log(Z_m/Z_0)$. These are finite-model quantities; their physical interpretation is conditional on the adopted preparation and transition assumptions.

For a protocol of [[def-td-driven-finite-path-model]], fix a bath temperature $T_b>0$ kelvin and set $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T_b)^{-1}$ in joules$^{-1}$, using the exact constant and SI conventions of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. The finite-state clause of the adopted [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] then gives the stage-zero law $\pi_0(i)=e^{-\beta E_0(i)}/Z_0$; adopt that the initial microstate is drawn from this law, so $\mu_0=\pi_0$. Here $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty and $E_0(i)$ is finite, so $0<Z_0<\infty$ as required by that clause. This is a model premise about the preparation distribution. It does not follow from the finite partition-sum definition, does not assert that an arbitrary system equilibrates in finite time, and does not report a measured preparation. The countable-state and measure-integral branches of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] are not used.

For the protocol in [[def-td-driven-finite-path-model]], adopt, at each stage $k=1,\ldots,m$, the stationarity condition $\sum_{i\in\Omega}\pi_k(i)K_k(i,j)=\pi_k(j)$ for every $j\in\Omega$. This says that if the bath transition begins with law $\pi_k$ at fixed energy $E_k$, it ends with the same law. It is a physical modeling assumption for this protocol family, not a consequence of the transition-kernel definition and not an assertion that the kernel mixes every initial law to $\pi_k$.

Assign a positive temperature $T$ in kelvins and the exact framework constant $k_{\mathrm B}$ in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ from [[def-td-si-quantities]], and put $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$. For a finite microstate model $(\Omega,\epsilon)$, adopt the canonical preparation
$$P_\beta(x)=\frac{e^{-\beta E(x)}}{Z(\beta)},\qquad Z(\beta)=\sum_{x\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E(x)}.$$
Here $Z$ is dimensionless, positive, and finite because $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty.

The same adopted law may be assigned to a specified countable state model with its stated enumeration and energy list, or to a measurable model $(X,\Sigma,\mu,E)$ with a dimensionless reference measure $\mu$ and measurable energy $E:X\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$, only when $0<Z(\beta)<\infty$ for the declared series or integral. In those cases $P_\beta(i)=e^{-\beta E_i}/Z$ or the probability density is $p_\beta=e^{-\beta E}/Z$ relative to $\mu$. The countable and integral conventions are those of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]] and [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]] at their actual current draft statements.

This is an adopted statistical-mechanical preparation rule. It is not derived from the macroscopic thermodynamic laws, a finite bath, entropy maximization, or a time-evolution equation. It does not assert that a physical sample has this preparation; that identification is an additional model assumption to be tested against a specified preparation and apparatus.

derivations.claim: For $k\ge1$ and $j\in\Omega$, define $S_k(j)$ by the finite sum over $i_0,\ldots,i_{k-1}\in\Omega$ of $\pi_0(i_0)\prod_{\ell=1}^kK_\ell(i_{\ell-1},i_\ell)e^{-\beta W_k}$, with $i_k=j$ and $W_k=\sum_{\ell=1}^k[E_\ell(i_{\ell-1})-E_{\ell-1}(i_{\ell-1})]$; put $S_0(j)=\pi_0(j)$. Partitioning this finite sum by the state $i=i_{k-1}$ gives $S_k(j)=\sum_iS_{k-1}(i)e^{-\beta(E_k(i)-E_{k-1}(i))}K_k(i,j)$. The canonical preparation gives the base $S_0(j)=\pi_0(j)=(Z_0/Z_0)\pi_0(j)$ by [A1] and the finite branch of [L1].
For the induction step fix $k\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and suppose $S_{k-1}(i)=(Z_{k-1}/Z_0)\pi_{k-1}(i)$ for every $i$.

Substitute this hypothesis in the recurrence from step 1.1. Since $\pi_{k-1}(i)=e^{-\beta E_{k-1}(i)}/Z_{k-1}$, the previous-stage Boltzmann factor cancels against the quench factor, giving $S_k(j)=(Z_k/Z_0)\sum_i\pi_k(i)K_k(i,j)=(Z_k/Z_0)\pi_k(j)$ by [A2]. This proves the induction step at each stage.

The base and induction step establish $S_k(j)=(Z_k/Z_0)\pi_k(j)$ for all stages. At $k=m$, summing over terminal states and using normalization of $\pi_m$ gives $\mathbb E_F[e^{-\beta W}]=Z_m/Z_0$. By $\Delta F=-\beta^{-1}\log(Z_m/Z_0)$, this equals $e^{-\beta\Delta F}$.

A finite rate model consists of a finite nonempty state set $S$ and rates $q_{ij}\ge0$ in seconds$^{-1}$ for $i\ne j$. Set $q_{ii}=-\sum_{j\ne i}q_{ij}$. citations.quote: Choose a Galilean inertial chart $\mathcal F$ as defined in [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]] for the specified fixed closed trap-and-bath body, assumed to have positive total mass and the center-of-mass map required there, and supply its componentwise differentiable center-of-mass trajectory on the whole modeled time interval. Assume that its center-of-mass velocity is one constant vector on that interval, so the single constant boost of that supplier selects $\mathcal F$ with zero center-of-mass velocity throughout. Take $\mathcal F$ to be this common rest chart. The trap-and-bath background is held fixed in this idealization; center-of-mass recoil or accelerating-frame dynamics are not part of the scalar process. In this chart let $\mathbf r_c\in\mathbb R^3$ be the fixed trap-center position and let $\mathbf e\in\mathbb R^3$ be a fixed unit vector along the modeled trap axis. For a particle position $\mathbf r\in\mathbb R^3$, define the signed displacement $x=\langle\mathbf r-\mathbf r_c,\mathbf e\rangle$ in metres; the process $X_t$ in [[def-tdmath-ornstein-uhlenbeck-equation]] is this coordinate of the particle position at time $t$. Thus $U(x)=kx^2/2$ is the harmonic potential relative to the trap center, not an absolute spatial coordinate. Using the SI conventions and exact $k_{\mathrm B}$ of [[def-td-si-quantities]], take stiffness $k>0$ in joules per square metre, constant mobility $\mu>0$ in square metres per joule-second, and bath temperature $T_b>0$ kelvin. Adopt the one-dimensional overdamped model $dX_t=-\gamma X_t\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t$, interpreted through the integral equation of [[def-tdmath-ornstein-uhlenbeck-equation]], with $\gamma=\mu k$ in seconds$^{-1}$ and $\sigma^2=2\mu k_{\mathrm B}T_b$ in square metres per second. Here $B$ is standard Brownian motion with its stated filtration and increment hypotheses, and the bath noise is independent of the initial preparation. This Einstein noise relation and the linear Markov model are physical assumptions. They do not follow from equilibrium thermodynamics alone and do not report a measured spectrum or calibration.

Assume the filtered probability space, Brownian increment hypothesis, and initial data of [[def-tdmath-ornstein-uhlenbeck-equation]], including $\mathbb E X_0^2<\infty$ and future increments independent of $\mathcal F_0$. For $\gamma,\sigma>0$, on every finite time interval the process
$$X_t=e^{-\gamma t}X_0+\sigma e^{-\gamma t}\int_0^t e^{\gamma s}\,dB_s$$
has a continuous adapted version, solves the stated Ornstein–Uhlenbeck integral equation, and is the unique continuous solution driven by the same $(X_0,B)$. Put $V=\sigma^2/(2\gamma)$. For $0\le s<t$, its transition law conditional on $\mathcal F_s$ is normal with mean $e^{-\gamma(t-s)}X_s$ and variance $V(1-e^{-2\gamma(t-s)})$. Consequently
$$\mathbb E X_t=e^{-\gamma t}\mathbb E X_0,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(X_t)=e^{-2\gamma t}\operatorname{Var}(X_0)+V(1-e^{-2\gamma t}).$$
From any such initial law, $X_t$ converges in distribution to $N(0,V)$. If $X_0\sim N(0,V)$ and is independent of future Brownian increments, the process is stationary Gaussian with covariance $C(\tau)=Ve^{-\gamma|\tau|}$, and its transition kernel satisfies detailed balance with the $N(0,V)$ density. Its transition density solves the Fokker–Planck equation for positive time. Under the convention $S(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R}C(\tau)e^{i\omega\tau}\,d\tau$, the stationary spectrum and time-average bound are
$$S(\omega)=\frac{V\gamma}{\pi(\gamma^2+\omega^2)},\qquad\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac1T\int_0^T X_t\,dt\right)\le\frac{2V}{\gamma T}.$$
All these statements concern the specified linear stochastic model. An Einstein relation between $\sigma$ and a physical bath temperature would be an additional physical postulate.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0},P)$ carry a standard Brownian motion $B$ adapted to the filtration, with future increments independent of the present sigma-algebra. Fix constants $\gamma>0$ and $\sigma>0$, and an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable real random variable $X_0$ with finite second moment. A **continuous adapted solution of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck equation** on $[0,T]$ is a continuous adapted process $X$ satisfying, almost surely for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$X_t=X_0-\gamma\int_0^tX_s\,ds+\sigma B_t,$$
where the time integral is the ordinary Lebesgue integral along the continuous path. In differential notation this is $dX_t=-\gamma X_t\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t$, with the stochastic differential interpreted through the displayed integral equation.

The definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. The Itô integral in the explicit representation is the square-integrable predictable-process integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]].

The inspected mathematical supplier's stationary clause applies with this $V$ and $\gamma=\mu k$, so $C(\tau)=Ve^{-\mu k|\tau|}$ and $S(\omega)=V\mu k/[\pi((\mu k)^2+\omega^2)]=\mu k_{\mathrm B}T_b/[\pi((\mu k)^2+\omega^2)]$.

citations.quote: Let $M$ be a finite memory-state set and $R$ a finite retained-register set. A joint preparation is a probability law $p(m,r)\ge0$ with $\sum_{m,r}p(m,r)=1$. Write $a_r=\sum_m p(m,r)$ and, for $a_r>0$, $q(m|r)=p(m,r)/a_r$. Use the finite Shannon entropy in nats and the conditional entropy $H(M|R)$ exactly as defined by [[lem-tdmath-conditional-memory-entropy]]. For a fixed target memory state $m_0$, a reset is the endpoint map $p'(m,r)=\mathbf 1_{\{m=m_0\}}a_r$: it places the memory at $m_0$ while leaving the register marginal unchanged. The definition alone assigns no physical entropy, work cost, heat transfer, or implementation.

Let $M$ and $R$ take values in finite sets under a joint probability law $p(m,r)\ge0$ with $\sum_{m,r}p(m,r)=1$. For any finite random variable $Y$ with law $p_Y$, define its Shannon entropy by $H(Y):=-\sum_{y:p_Y(y)>0}p_Y(y)\log p_Y(y)$; for a pair, $H(M,R)$ means this definition applied to its joint law. Put $a_r:=\sum_m p(m,r)$ and, when $a_r>0$, $q(m|r):=p(m,r)/a_r$. Thus $H(R)=-\sum_{r:a_r>0}a_r\log a_r$. Define $H(M|R):=\sum_{r:a_r>0}a_r[-\sum_{m:q(m|r)>0}q(m|r)\log q(m|r)]$. Then $H(M,R)=H(R)+H(M|R)$ and $H(M|R)\ge0$.

derivations.claim: Initially the memory-register entropy is $k_{\mathrm B}[H(R)+H(M|R)]$ by [F2] and [A1]. After reset, the memory is deterministic conditional on each register value, so $H(M'|R)=0$; applying the same finite entropy chain rule gives final entropy $k_{\mathrm B}H(R)$.
Therefore $\Delta S_{\mathrm{memory+register}}=-k_{\mathrm B}H(M|R)$. Substitution into [A4] gives $Q_b\ge k_{\mathrm B}T_bH(M|R)$ because $T_b>0$.

By the adopted endpoint first-law convention [A3], $W=Q_b$, so $W\ge k_{\mathrm B}T_bH(M|R)$. The conclusion is conditional on [A1]--[A4]; the entropy bound alone does not assert that the reset can be implemented reversibly or that every bit erasure costs $k_{\mathrm B}T_b\log2$.

citations.quote:
Take $\Omega$ to be a finite nonempty microstate set as in [[def-td-finite-microstate-model]]: distinct elements count as distinct microstates, and the physical energy values are finite and measured in joules in the declared rest frame. For the physical internal-energy interpretation, use one declared fixed Galilean chart for every stage, with the bulk center-of-mass and separately tracked external-energy sectors suppressed from this finite protocol. The companion mechanical model supplies the center-of-mass data required by the microstate supplier; when the common chart is called a center-of-mass rest chart throughout the protocol, its center-of-mass velocity is constant over the modeled interval, and one constant boost selects that chart. This fixed-chart idealization does not infer a rest chart from the finite set or transition kernels, and does not describe an accelerating bulk body. Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and stage energy functions $E_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$ for $k=0,\ldots,m$, with the energy offsets fixed by the declared protocol model. Fix inverse temperature $\beta>0$ in joules$^{-1}$. The finite partition sum and canonical probability vector at stage $k$ are $Z_k=\sum_{i\in\Omega}e^{-\beta E_k(i)}$ and $\pi_k(i)=e^{-\beta E_k(i)}/Z_k$. Since $\Omega$ is nonempty and finite and each energy is finite, $0<Z_k<\infty$ and $\pi_k$ is a strictly positive probability vector.

A transition kernel at stage $k$ is a matrix $K_k(i,j)\ge0$ with $\sum_{j\in\Omega}K_k(i,j)=1$. In the forward stage order, the energy changes instantaneously from $E_{k-1}$ to $E_k$ while the state is still $i_{k-1}$; the subsequent bath transition samples $i_k$ using $K_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$ at fixed energy $E_k$. A path is $\omega=(i_0,\ldots,i_m)\in\Omega^{m+1}$. The initial law is a probability vector $\mu_0:\Omega\to[0,1]$ with $\sum_{i\in\Omega}\mu_0(i)=1$. Its path probability is $P_F(\omega)=\mu_0(i_0)\prod_{k=1}^mK_k(i_{k-1},i_k)$; summing over all paths gives $1$ by the normalization of $\mu_0$ and the row sums of the kernels.

Work on the system is positive when energy is supplied to it, and heat into the system is positive when a bath transition raises its energy. Define $W(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_{k-1})-E_{k-1}(i_{k-1})]$ and $Q_{\mathrm{in}}(\omega)=\sum_{k=1}^m[E_k(i_k)-E_k(i_{k-1})]$, both in joules. Define $F_k=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_k$ and $\Delta F=F_m-F_0=-\beta^{-1}\log(Z_m/Z_0)$. These are finite-model quantities; their physical interpretation is conditional on the adopted preparation and transition assumptions.

For a protocol of [[def-td-driven-finite-path-model]], fix a bath temperature $T_b>0$ kelvin and set $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T_b)^{-1}$ in joules$^{-1}$, using the exact constant and SI conventions of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. The finite-state clause of the adopted [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] then gives the stage-zero law $\pi_0(i)=e^{-\beta E_0(i)}/Z_0$; adopt that the initial microstate is drawn from this law, so $\mu_0=\pi_0$. Here $\Omega$ is finite and nonempty and $E_0(i)$ is finite, so $0<Z_0<\infty$ as required by that clause. This is a model premise about the preparation distribution. It does not follow from the finite partition-sum definition, does not assert that an arbitrary system equilibrates in finite time, and does not report a measured preparation. The countable-state and measure-integral branches of [[post-td-canonical-sampling]] are not used.

For the forward path law of [[def-td-driven-finite-path-model]], under [[post-td-canonical-protocol-preparation]] and [[post-td-stationary-bath-kernel]], the finite expectation satisfies $\mathbb E_F[e^{-\beta W}]=Z_m/Z_0=e^{-\beta\Delta F}$. This is an ensemble identity; it does not say $W=\Delta F$ on each path.

A finite rate model consists of a finite nonempty state set $S$ and rates $q_{ij}\ge0$ in seconds$^{-1}$ for $i\ne j$. Set $q_{ii}=-\sum_{j\ne i}q_{ij}$. A row probability vector is $p=(p_i)_{i\in S}$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$; write $\Delta(S)=\{p\in[0,1]^S:\sum_i p_i=1\}$. A time-dependent law is a coordinatewise continuously differentiable map $p:[0,\infty)\to\Delta(S)$, with a right derivative at $t=0$, that satisfies the continuous-time master equation $\dot p_i(t)=\sum_{j\ne i}[p_j(t)q_{ji}-p_i(t)q_{ij}]$ for every $t\ge0$. A strictly positive normalized vector $\pi$ is a detailed-balance law when $\pi_iq_{ij}=\pi_jq_{ji}$ for every distinct pair. Its undirected rate graph has an edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $\pi_iq_{ij}>0$; detailed balance makes this equivalent to $\pi_jq_{ji}>0$.

On a finite nonempty state set $S$, a discrete transition kernel is a matrix $K:S\times S\to[0,1]$ satisfying $\sum_{j\in S}K(i,j)=1$ for every $i\in S$. For a strictly positive row probability vector $\pi\in\Delta(S)$, the kernel satisfies $\pi$-detailed balance when $\pi_iK(i,j)=\pi_jK(j,i)$ for every $i,j\in S$. This identity pairs the supports of forward and reversed transitions. A rate model or a reversible kernel is a mathematical/physical model class; no observed trajectory is asserted by the definition.

Let $S$ have $N\ge2$ states, positive detailed-balance law $\pi$, and connected undirected rate graph as in [[def-td-detailed-balance-rate-model]]. For every strictly positive initial probability vector $p(0)$, the master equation has a unique strictly positive probability solution $p(t)$ for all $t\ge0$. The relative entropy $D(p(t)\Vert\pi)=\sum_i p_i(t)\log(p_i(t)/\pi_i)$ is nonincreasing, and $p_i(t)\to\pi_i$ for every state. No monotonicity of Shannon entropy $-\sum_i p_i\log p_i$ is asserted.

derivations.claim: The third probability is constant and $p_1+p_2=1/2$. The difference $d=p_1-p_2$ satisfies $\dot d=-2d$ with $d(0)=1/4$, so $d(t)=e^{-2t}/4$, $p_1(t)=1/4+e^{-2t}/8$, and $p_2(t)=1/4-e^{-2t}/8$.
Hence $p(t)\to(1/4,1/4,1/2)\ne\pi$. The relative entropy tends to $\frac12\log(9/8)>0$, confirming that detailed balance without connectedness does not force convergence to the full reference law.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

citations.quote: Choose a Galilean inertial chart $\mathcal F$ as defined in [[def-td-galilean-rest-frame]] for the specified fixed closed trap-and-bath body, assumed to have positive total mass and the center-of-mass map required there, and supply its componentwise differentiable center-of-mass trajectory on the whole modeled time interval. Assume that its center-of-mass velocity is one constant vector on that interval, so the single constant boost of that supplier selects $\mathcal F$ with zero center-of-mass velocity throughout. Take $\mathcal F$ to be this common rest chart. The trap-and-bath background is held fixed in this idealization; center-of-mass recoil or accelerating-frame dynamics are not part of the scalar process. In this chart let $\mathbf r_c\in\mathbb R^3$ be the fixed trap-center position and let $\mathbf e\in\mathbb R^3$ be a fixed unit vector along the modeled trap axis. For a particle position $\mathbf r\in\mathbb R^3$, define the signed displacement $x=\langle\mathbf r-\mathbf r_c,\mathbf e\rangle$ in metres; the process $X_t$ in [[def-tdmath-ornstein-uhlenbeck-equation]] is this coordinate of the particle position at time $t$. Thus $U(x)=kx^2/2$ is the harmonic potential relative to the trap center, not an absolute spatial coordinate. Using the SI conventions and exact $k_{\mathrm B}$ of [[def-td-si-quantities]], take stiffness $k>0$ in joules per square metre, constant mobility $\mu>0$ in square metres per joule-second, and bath temperature $T_b>0$ kelvin. Adopt the one-dimensional overdamped model $dX_t=-\gamma X_t\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t$, interpreted through the integral equation of [[def-tdmath-ornstein-uhlenbeck-equation]], with $\gamma=\mu k$ in seconds$^{-1}$ and $\sigma^2=2\mu k_{\mathrm B}T_b$ in square metres per second. Here $B$ is standard Brownian motion with its stated filtration and increment hypotheses, and the bath noise is independent of the initial preparation. This Einstein noise relation and the linear Markov model are physical assumptions. They do not follow from equilibrium thermodynamics alone and do not report a measured spectrum or calibration.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. It is inherited from the Brownian and Itô-integral suppliers used for the stationary Gaussian model.

Under [[post-td-linear-ornstein-uhlenbeck-bath]], prepare $X_0\sim N(0,V)$ independently of future Brownian increments, where $V=k_{\mathrm B}T_b/k$. Then the conditional linear model has stationary covariance $C(\tau)=Ve^{-\mu k|\tau|}$. With angular-frequency convention $S(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R}C(\tau)e^{i\omega\tau}\,d\tau$, its spectrum is $S(\omega)=\mu k_{\mathrm B}T_b/(\pi[(\mu k)^2+\omega^2])$. For every averaging time $T>0$, $\operatorname{Var}(T^{-1}\int_0^T X_t\,dt)\le 2k_{\mathrm B}T_b/(\mu k^2T)$. These are model predictions, not reported observations.

derivations.claim: Substituting $V=k_{\mathrm B}T_b/k$ and $\gamma=\mu k$ into the exact spectrum supplied by [F2] gives $S(\omega)=\mu k_{\mathrm B}T_b/(\pi[(\mu k)^2+\omega^2])$.

The same supplier bound becomes $\operatorname{Var}(T^{-1}\int_0^T X_tdt)\le2k_{\mathrm B}T_b/(\mu k^2T)$, which tends to zero as $T\to\infty$. Both formulas are conditional model predictions, not measurements.

citations.quote: Let $M$ be a finite memory-state set and $R$ a finite retained-register set. A joint preparation is a probability law $p(m,r)\ge0$ with $\sum_{m,r}p(m,r)=1$. Write $a_r=\sum_m p(m,r)$ and, for $a_r>0$, $q(m|r)=p(m,r)/a_r$. Use the finite Shannon entropy in nats and the conditional entropy $H(M|R)$ exactly as defined by [[lem-tdmath-conditional-memory-entropy]]. For a fixed target memory state $m_0$, a reset is the endpoint map $p'(m,r)=\mathbf 1_{\{m=m_0\}}a_r$: it places the memory at $m_0$ while leaving the register marginal unchanged. The definition alone assigns no physical entropy, work cost, heat transfer, or implementation.

For the reset model of [[def-td-finite-memory-reset-model]], use the exact SI value and conventions of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. Assume (i) the dimensionless Shannon entropies in nats from [[lem-tdmath-conditional-memory-entropy]] give memory-register thermodynamic entropy $S_{\mathrm{memory+register}}=k_{\mathrm B}H(M,R)$ in joules per kelvin at both endpoints, with $k_{\mathrm B}$ in joules per kelvin, (ii) a single ideal reservoir remains at fixed temperature $T_b>0$ kelvin and receives heat $Q_b$ in joules, (iii) the memory-register endpoint energy is unchanged so the adopted first-law convention gives work on the system $W=Q_b$ in joules, and (iv) the total entropy change obeys $\Delta S_{\mathrm{memory+register}}+Q_b/T_b\ge0$ in joules per kelvin. Then $W\ge k_{\mathrm B}T_bH(M|R)$, with both sides in joules. Equality is not asserted without a separately specified reversible implementation.

derivations.claim: Substitution into the conditional reset theorem gives $H(M|R)=H(M)=-p\log p-(1-p)\log(1-p)$.
Therefore the theorem gives $W\ge k_{\mathrm B}T_b[-p\log p-(1-p)\log(1-p)]$ for this preparation. It reports no work measurement and makes no claim about an apparatus.

citations.quote: Let $M$ and $R$ take values in finite sets under a joint probability law $p(m,r)\ge0$ with $\sum_{m,r}p(m,r)=1$. For any finite random variable $Y$ with law $p_Y$, define its Shannon entropy by $H(Y):=-\sum_{y:p_Y(y)>0}p_Y(y)\log p_Y(y)$; for a pair, $H(M,R)$ means this definition applied to its joint law. Put $a_r:=\sum_m p(m,r)$ and, when $a_r>0$, $q(m|r):=p(m,r)/a_r$. Thus $H(R)=-\sum_{r:a_r>0}a_r\log a_r$. Define $H(M|R):=\sum_{r:a_r>0}a_r[-\sum_{m:q(m|r)>0}q(m|r)\log q(m|r)]$. Then $H(M,R)=H(R)+H(M|R)$ and $H(M|R)\ge0$.

For the reset model of [[def-td-finite-memory-reset-model]], use the exact SI value and conventions of [[def-td-si-quantities]]. Assume (i) the dimensionless Shannon entropies in nats from [[lem-tdmath-conditional-memory-entropy]] give memory-register thermodynamic entropy $S_{\mathrm{memory+register}}=k_{\mathrm B}H(M,R)$ in joules per kelvin at both endpoints, with $k_{\mathrm B}$ in joules per kelvin, (ii) a single ideal reservoir remains at fixed temperature $T_b>0$ kelvin and receives heat $Q_b$ in joules, (iii) the memory-register endpoint energy is unchanged so the adopted first-law convention gives work on the system $W=Q_b$ in joules, and (iv) the total entropy change obeys $\Delta S_{\mathrm{memory+register}}+Q_b/T_b\ge0$ in joules per kelvin. Then $W\ge k_{\mathrm B}T_bH(M|R)$, with both sides in joules. Equality is not asserted without a separately specified reversible implementation.

derivations.claim: The memory marginal is uniform, so $H(M)=\log2$. Given either value of $R$, the conditional law of $M$ is a point mass; hence each conditional entropy is zero and $H(M|R)=0$.

Therefore the theorem yields only $W\ge0$ for this reset under its stated thermodynamic assumptions, while the unconditioned memory entropy is $\log2$. It does not imply a $k_{\mathrm B}T_b\log2$ lower bound for this correlated preparation.
